extracted.intended_audience: regulatory analysts and decisionmakers in U.S. federal agencies (heads of executive agencies and establishments)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing regulatory analyses required under Executive Order 12866 and related statutes: how to structure, quantify, document, and present benefits, costs, alternatives, and specialized analyses for major federal rulemakings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key elements of a regulatory analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: A good regulatory analysis should include: (1) a statement of the need for the proposed action, (2) an examination of alternative approaches, and (3) an evaluation of the benefits and costs—quantitative and qualitative—of the proposed action and the main alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also explain how actions are linked to expected benefits, identify a baseline (normally 'no action'), and identify expected undesirable side-effects and ancillary benefits. Present a summary of benefit and cost estimates for each alternative including qualitative and non-monetized factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of the need for Federal regulatory action
rubrics_metrics.description: Before recommending Federal regulatory action, an agency must demonstrate that the proposed action is necessary, describe statutory authority and discretion, and identify and assess the significance of the problem to be addressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain whether action addresses market failure or other compelling public need; quantify failures where feasible; show government intervention is likely to do more good than harm; document strengths and limitations of intangible rationales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market failure or other social purpose justification
rubrics_metrics.description: If regulation is to correct market failures, the analysis should describe the failure (externality, market power, inadequate/asymmetric information, common property/public goods) qualitatively and where feasible quantitatively. Other rationales (improving government functioning, redistribution, anti-discrimination, privacy) are permissible but should be examined for effectiveness and cost-effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume market failure; document inadequacy of private market responses. If information-processing errors are claimed, provide careful documentation. Consider alternative non-regulatory solutions before regulating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Showing federal level is best
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should consider whether Federal regulation is the appropriate level of government action and weigh alternatives such as state/local regulation, antitrust, litigation, or administrative compensation systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess spillover characteristics (e.g., interstate effects), costs of fragmented state rules, benefits of harmonization for global markets, and whether state/local experimentation could be preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption against certain economic regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: A particularly demanding burden of proof is required to justify: price controls in competitive markets; production or sales quotas in competitive markets; mandatory uniform quality standards when voluntary standards or disclosure suffice; controls on entry into employment or production (with stated exceptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid regulation that increases market power; justify exceptions (natural monopoly, health/safety requirements) carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of a meaningful set of alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Once regulation is appropriate, analyze a manageable but sufficiently broad set of alternatives, including reasonable modifications of the regulation's attributes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance thoroughness against analytical capacity; eliminate some alternatives preliminarily but justify the remaining set for detailed analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different choices defined by statute
rubrics_metrics.description: When statutes set specific requirements and agencies consider standards more stringent than statutory minima, examine benefits and costs of alternatives within the agency's statutory discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include alternatives reflecting the full range of reasonable statutory interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different compliance dates
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess how the timing of compliance affects net benefits; different compliance dates may substantially change costs and benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider lead times for industries, lost future benefits from delayed implementation, and whether phased or staggered dates reduce overall costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different enforcement methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate alternative enforcement and monitoring methods (on-site inspections, periodic reporting, penalties, random monitoring, parametric monitoring) for cost-effectiveness and appropriateness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the enforcement framework that provides appropriate incentives at lowest cost; consider Federal/State/local enforcement mixes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different degrees of stringency
rubrics_metrics.description: Study multiple levels of regulatory stringency because both benefits and costs typically increase with stringency; marginal benefits may fall as stringency increases while marginal costs may rise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze how stringency affects size and distribution of benefits and costs and present incremental estimates across levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different requirements for different sized firms
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider differential requirements based on firm size due to varying compliance costs and impacts; recognize small firms may face higher per-unit compliance burdens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid imposing heavier burdens on productive firms solely because they can better afford compliance; account for Regulatory Flexibility Act requirements when impacts on substantial numbers of small entities are likely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different requirements for different geographic regions
rubrics_metrics.description: Where regional variations in benefits or costs are significant, consider regional differentiation of requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance efficiency gains from tailored regional rules against costs of fragmentation and compliance with multiple jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance standards rather than design standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer outcome-based (performance) standards to prescriptive design/engineering standards because performance standards allow flexibility for cost-effective compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for monitoring/compliance costs associated with flexibility; evaluate tradeoffs between flexibility and enforceability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market-oriented approaches rather than direct controls
rubrics_metrics.description: Explore market-based mechanisms (fees, penalties, subsidies, tradable permits/offsets, changes to liability/property rights, bonds/insurance/warranties) as potentially lower-cost alternatives to command-and-control regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider averaging, banking, trading programs (ABT) for emissions if they do not produce unacceptable local 'hot spots'; assess distributional and implementation complexities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informational measures rather than regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: When failures stem from inadequate/asymmetric information, prefer informational remedies (standardized testing/rating, mandatory disclosure, government provision of information) where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate full costs of mandatory disclosures (gathering, communicating, crowding out other info, misinterpretation, perverse incentives). Consider the least intrusive informational alternative adequate to the objective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of benefit-cost analysis (BCA)
rubrics_metrics.description: When benefits and costs can be monetized, express them in monetary units to identify the most efficient alternative (maximizing net benefits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure incremental benefits and costs, avoid using benefit-cost ratios as indicators of net benefits, present physical units where monetization is not possible, avoid double-counting, provide sensitivity and uncertainty analyses, and use professional judgment where non-monetized factors matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of cost-effectiveness analysis (CEA)
rubrics_metrics.description: For rulemakings where primary benefits are health/safety and a valid effectiveness measure exists, prepare a CEA; perform BCA for major rulemakings where monetary values can be assigned to primary health/safety outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer final outcomes (lives saved, life-years saved) over intermediate outputs; use integrated measures (ELs, QALYs) when appropriate; be cautious with average cost-effectiveness ratios and prefer incremental cost-effectiveness analysis; ensure effectiveness metrics appropriately weight consequences and consider multiple outcomes carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost and effectiveness measurement construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct cost measures to include all relevant societal costs (public and private) and define the numerator of CEA as net costs (gross compliance costs minus cost savings). Choose effectiveness measures that capture final outcomes and account for variability in quality of measured units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid double-counting benefits/costs across numerator and denominator; explain choice of effectiveness measure; when multiple outcomes exist, weight appropriately or monetize if possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incremental analysis and dominance principles
rubrics_metrics.description: When comparing alternatives, present incremental benefits/costs and incremental cost-effectiveness relative to successively more stringent alternatives; eliminate inferior alternatives by strong/weak dominance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether alternatives are mutually exclusive or can be combined; consider regulatory budget constraints when comparing combinable options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of benefits and costs over time (discounting and reporting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Present undiscounted streams of annual benefit and cost estimates for each year of the analytic horizon and present annualized benefits and costs using real discount rates of 3% and 7%. Report monetized effects in a specified base year (2001 dollars in the Circular).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start streams in the year the final rule will begin to have effects; convert dollar years to the base-year using the GDP deflator; report both undiscounted and annualized figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of risk and uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide expected-value estimates and, where available, distributions around estimates (e.g., 5th and 95th percentiles). Where only bounds are available, present appropriate confidence bounds and describe results under plausible alternative assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply full disclosure and transparency; where assumptions critically affect conclusions, present benefits and costs under alternative plausible assumptions and perform sensitivity analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision and rounding of estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Reported estimates should reflect feasible precision. Rounding implies precision (e.g., $220 million rounded to nearest $10 million implies +/- $5 million).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose rounding consistent with underlying precision and document implied margins of error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate reporting of transfers
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and report transfer payments separately and avoid misclassifying transfers as benefits or costs; distinguish transfers caused by Federal budget actions from transfers between non-governmental parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use categories sufficient to describe major redistributive effects; identify transfers that have significant efficiency effects in addition to distributional effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting statement and standardized tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide an accounting statement with tables reporting benefit and cost estimates for each major final rule, using the Circular's suggested format and categories (monetized quantified; monetized but not quantified; qualitative but not quantified or monetized).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid double-counting; provide documentation footnotes and warnings as needed; include annualized and undiscounted streams, confidence bounds where possible, and alternate mortality valuation estimates when applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantifying and monetizing benefits and costs
rubrics_metrics.description: To the extent feasible, quantify all incremental benefits and costs and convert to dollar amounts. When physical units can be measured they should be reported even if not monetized; when monetization is possible, convert quantified estimates to monetary equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When some benefits/costs cannot be monetized, report them qualitatively and, if important, perform threshold (break-even) analysis to evaluate their significance relative to net benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold or break-even analysis for non-quantified effects
rubrics_metrics.description: When important benefits or costs are not monetized, carry out threshold/break-even analysis to determine how small/large the non-quantified values would have to be to change the net benefit sign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicate which non-quantified effects are most important and why; use threshold analysis to inform decisionmakers about potential significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valuation of mortality and alternative primary estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Present alternative primary estimates where different values are used for reductions in premature mortality risk (e.g., alternative VSL estimates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report sensitivity to different mortality valuations; document methods and rationale for chosen values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption on risk preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: In general assume risk neutrality in analysis unless there is justification for a different assumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If adopting a different risk preference assumption, explain reasons and implications for results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of distributional effects and identification of shares
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify how benefits, costs, and transfers are distributed, including portions received by State, local, and tribal governments, small businesses, wages, and effects on economic growth where feasible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note that rules with annual costs under $1 billion are likely to have minimal effect on economic growth; report distributional impacts separately where significant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialized statutory and executive-order analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider and, where required, prepare specialized analyses: Regulatory Flexibility Act analyses (impacts on small entities), Unfunded Mandates Act statements (for >$100M impacts), Paperwork Reduction Act analyses (information collection burdens), Information Quality Guidelines, NEPA environmental impact statements, EO 13045 impacts on children, and EO 13211 energy effects statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the specific statutory thresholds, consult agency counsel and CIO as appropriate, post RFAs online, notify SBA Chief Counsel for Advocacy as required, and publish energy statements or summaries in NPRMs and final rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information quality and data/documentation standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Data and analysis supporting the rule must meet agency and OMB information quality standards; provide specific references to sources, appendices documenting models, and results of formal sensitivity and uncertainty analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency CIO and OMB offices can assist; ensure transparency so qualified third parties can see how estimates and conclusions were derived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stakeholder consultation and early engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek opinions of those affected by regulation and those with special knowledge early in the analytic process to ensure relevant issues and data are addressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not limit consultation to final stages; consult widely (including those not directly affected) to access pertinent data and perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive summary and supporting appendices
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory analyses should include an executive summary and standardized accounting statement, with appendices that document models, data sources, and detailed analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make appendices available to support transparency; include documentation of assumptions, sensitivity analyses, and references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness considerations in effectiveness measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: When selecting effectiveness metrics (especially for public health/safety), adjust measures as appropriate to ensure fair treatment of all population segments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider use of integrated measures (ELs, QALYs) but be mindful of restrictive assumptions underlying them and their implications for different groups; explain and justify choices to ensure fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding misleading indicators (ratios and averages)
rubrics_metrics.description: Benefit-cost ratios and average cost-effectiveness ratios are not meaningful indicators of net benefits and can be misleading; incremental comparisons are preferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not base decisions solely on benefit-cost ratios or average CEA; use incremental net benefits or incremental cost-effectiveness comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding double-counting and consistency across analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure consistency in estimation across regulations and avoid double-counting benefits or costs (e.g., not counting a life-saving valuation both as a monetary benefit and as part of effectiveness in the denominator).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully construct cost and effectiveness measures, make hidden assumptions explicit, and maintain consistency to achieve efficient allocation of risk-reduction resources.
